name: Eriochloa

look_here_first: TEXAS CUPGRASS: 1) big upright PERENNIAL bunch, 2) at the actual INNER leaf/sheath junction a dense ligule FRINGE of straight hairs, 3) narrow flowering panicle with several SHORT upright branches pressed along a central hairy axis, 4) on a mature 3.6–4.2 mm spikelet inspect the tiny cup-shaped CALLUS where it attaches to its short hairy pedicel under 10–20×. Crew, do not mistake a whole head for the tiny cup, or label a visible zigzag axis as proof without a connected spikelet!

recognition.where_to_look_first: Whole bunch → collar true ligule → narrow flowering head → one mature spikelet and its tiny basal cup/ring with 10–20× lens.
priority: perennial tuft from fibrous root mass, lacking creeping rhizomes
dense ring of straight hairs at ligule rather than a membrane
closely appressed slender racemes with soft/silky spikelets
small cup-like ring at each spikelet's base, requiring macro
zigzag remnant axis after spikelets drop (when seen)

comparison_lesson.memory_rule: BUNCH → HAIR LIGULE → FUZZY SEEDHEAD → TRUE SPIKELET CUP (macro).
quick_split: E. sericea — tufted perennial commonly about 0.3–1.2 m; soft blades, ring of straight ligular hairs, small fuzzy clustered spikelets on short hair-bearing stalks; tiny cup at spikelet base.
Paspalum spp. — can have spikelets in one-sided racemes but lack the diagnostic Eriochloa cup-like lower attachment; their ligule is generally membranous rather than a dense hair ring.
Digitaria spp. — often spreading grasses with fingerlike racemes and paired spikelets; no Eriochloa cup at each spikelet base. Inspect the same-plant base and spikelet attachments.
Panicum spp. — open or contracted panicles, but do not share the cup-like spikelet base; check spikelet, stalk, ligule with magnification.
comparison_lesson.range_guardrail: The existing Texas-native treatment is not a certified Hays County BONAP/NAPA determination; do not alter native_target_zone fields.

what_to_teach_crew: The 'cup' is a tiny structure right UNDER each individual spikelet, not a cup-shaped flowering head.
This genus lesson currently includes only E. sericea; do not extrapolate its exact measurements to every global Eriochloa species.
Have the crew trace the lateral flowering branches along the main axis; a handful of green spikelets over a finger only proves a flowering head, not its identification.
The real ligule is a hair fringe INSIDE the blade–sheath junction. Do not mislabel hairs elsewhere on the plant.
Kew's accepted E. sericea treatment describes 4–10 approximately 1.5–3-cm racemes and 3.6–4.2-mm individual spikelets. Flowering unit, branch and plant all require DIFFERENT scales.
Tiny cup not visible? Record 'cupgrass suspected' and photograph one intact spikelet with a real 1-mm reference before claiming species confirmation.
Avoid confusing Paspalum or Digitaria, which have different spikelet attachments and generally membranous ligules; confirm actual specimen anatomy rather than color.
Do not publish Noble, Texas A&M, seed nursery, or USDA handbook figure JPEGs on public site without individual photo reuse rights.

visual_comparison.title: ERIOCHLOA / CUPGRASSES — see the real head; inspect the hidden cup
visual_comparison.subtitle: Three existing, locally archived, individually credited Texas cupgrass real photographs now teach green and dry heads with five original broad visible-structure arrows. Critical ligule hair ring and 3.6–4.2-mm spikelet basal cup NOT photographed; no speculative macro arrows. visual_comparison.memory_rule: BUNCH → HAIR-FRINGE LIGULE → SHORT ONE-SIDED RACEMES → TINY CUP UNDER ONE SPIKELET (10–20×).

items.label: REAL CUPGRASS CUP — pale globular base beneath detached spikelet; Bob Harms, Texas
items.image_role: ACTUAL E. sericea detached spikelets with visibly pale globular basal cup/callus and original photographed scale reference

items.caption: Original Selected Central Texas Monocots ERSE5-9 photo by Bob Harms. In the LOWER RIGHT, a pale rounded CUP-LIKE CALLUS is visible below one detached spikelet; the arrow marks the actual pale basal knob, and a second arrow marks the spikelet body ABOVE it. The upper source scale strip is photographed, not generated. Do NOT call this an in-situ attached hairy pedicel, an actual ligule, or calibrated cup diameter. items.why_it_matters: Finally shows why Texas cupgrass is called a cupgrass: a tiny rounded/globular base belongs BELOW a single spikelet, NOT to the flowering head. Other grasses with narrow racemes can look similar until actual spikelet bases are checked.
items.photo_status: FIRST REAL visible source-authenticated E. sericea basal cup/callus photo; detached units, no attached pedicel or precision mm measurement. Existing true ligule and rooted whole-plant photo gaps preserved.

quick_field_id_tiles.heading: 01 · FIND THE BUNCH
quick_field_id_tiles.cue: Erect robust perennial tuft, usually 0.3–1.2 m
quick_field_id_tiles.expand: Photograph the rooted crown and lower sheaths. Texas cupgrass is caespitose (tufted) and lacks long rhizomes. Other bunchgrasses can mimic habit, so crown alone is not proof.

quick_field_id_tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN THE COLLAR
quick_field_id_tiles.cue: Ligule = tight fringe of straight hairs, not a membrane
quick_field_id_tiles.expand: Fold the blade aside and magnify the actual inner blade/sheath junction at 10–20×. Hairs on leaf margins, sheath or nodes are NOT the true ligule. The available Noble grass-photo reference is study-only until rights are verified.

quick_field_id_tiles.heading: 03 · FOLLOW THE FLOWER HEAD
quick_field_id_tiles.cue: Narrow central axis with 4–10 short, erect, one-sided side racemes
quick_field_id_tiles.expand: Kew describes the individual racemes as about 1.5–3 cm and the spikelets in two rows, on hairy short pedicels. Three real source-credited photos show broad green and dry flowering-head outlines. Current markers indicate gross axis and lateral units, NOT the tiny cup.

quick_field_id_tiles.heading: 04 · PROVE THE CUP
quick_field_id_tiles.cue: Single 3.6–4.2 mm spikelet has a globular callus / cup at its base
quick_field_id_tiles.expand: Use 10–20× (prefer 20–40×) and a 1-mm reference with one individual spikelet still attached to the hairy pedicel. This is NOT a cup-shaped seedhead; it is a tiny ring/swell just underneath the spikelet. Kew identifies a globular spikelet callus incorporating the basal rachilla internode. Now see source-credited original ERSE5-9 photo: pale rounded callus UNDER a detached spikelet. The visible white knob has an accurate arrow; NOT the same as showing an intact attached plant pedicel.
quick_field_id_tiles.photo_status: ACTUAL DETACHED BASAL CUP PHOTOGRAPH NOW PRESENT; ATTACHED PEDICEL + MEASURED 1-MM REFERENCE STILL MISSING
